title: What a layer costs
objectives: Count the parameters and multiply-adds of a convolutional layer, and compare them with a dense one.

screens.title: Two layers, one job
screens.prose: Both layers turn an 8 by 8 image into 16 maps of 8 by 8. One is a 3 by 3 convolution with 16 filters and padding 1. The other is a dense layer from the 64 pixels to all $16 \times 64 = 1{,}024$ outputs, each with its own weights and bias.
screens.question: Roughly how many times more parameters does the dense layer have?

options.why: Each dense output has 64 weights of its own; each conv filter has 9 shared by every position.
Count the dense layer: $64 \times 1{,}024$ weights alone is over 65,000.
The conv layer has 160 parameters, not 16.

hints.text: How many weights does one conv filter hold?
The dense layer: $64 \times 1{,}024$ weights plus 1,024 biases.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count both: weights per output, times outputs, plus biases.

explain.text: The convolution has $16 \times (9 + 1) = 160$; the dense layer $64 \times 1{,}024 + 1{,}024 = 66{,}560$. The convolution reuses each 3 by 3 kernel at all 64 positions.

screens.title: Channels in, channels out
screens.prose: Slide the number of input and output channels. The bars show both layers’ parameters, for 3 by 3 kernels on an 8 by 8 image, on a log scale.

derive.caption: {{cin}} in, {{cout}} out: conv {{cout * (cin * 9 + 1)}}, dense {{64 * cin * 64 * cout + 64 * cout}}

screens.question: With 8 channels in and 16 out, how many parameters does the convolution have?

hints.text: Read the conv bar or the caption.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each filter has a 3 by 3 kernel for every input channel, plus one bias.

byKey.no-cin: That is one input channel. Each filter has a kernel per input channel.

explain.text: Each filter holds $8 \times 9 = 72$ weights and 1 bias; 16 filters make 1,168. The image size never appears.

screens.title: Counting a layer
screens.prose: A convolutional layer with $c_{\text{in}}$ input channels and $c_{\text{out}}$ filters of $k \times k$ has $$c_{\text{out}}(c_{\text{in}} k^2 + 1)$$ parameters, whatever the image size: **parameter sharing**. A dense layer from $n_{\text{in}}$ to $n_{\text{out}}$ has $n_{\text{in}} n_{\text{out}} + n_{\text{out}}$, as `stat-learning` counted for a 2-2-1 net.
screens.question: How many parameters does the dense layer from the 64 pixels to 1,024 outputs have?

hints.text: Every one of 64 inputs joins every one of 1,024 outputs.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Weights from every input to every output, then one bias per output.

byKey.one-map: That is 64 outputs, one map. There are 16 maps of 64.

explain.text: $65{,}536$ weights and $1{,}024$ biases: 66,560, against 160 for the convolution that does the same shapes.

screens.title: What a layer costs to run
screens.prose: Parameters measure what a layer must learn; **multiply-adds** measure what it costs to run. Each output value of a convolution is a dot product of $k^2 c_{\text{in}}$ terms, and there is one per position per filter.
screens.question: The 1-to-16 convolution on an 8 by 8 image with padding 1: how many multiply-adds?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Positions times terms per dot product times filters.

byKey.one-filter: That is one filter. There are 16.
byKey.params: That is the parameter count. Each weight is used at all 64 positions.

explain.text: 64 positions, 9 terms each, 16 filters: 9,216. Each of the 144 weights is used 64 times: cheap to store, and still cheaper to run than the dense layer.

screens.title: The net of level 3
screens.prose: Level 3 trains this net on 8 by 8 digits. A 3 by 3 convolution has 16 filters and padding 1; 2 by 2 max pooling leaves 4 by 4 by 16; a dense layer gives 10 classes.
screens.question: Fill in the parameters of each layer and the total.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Pooling has no parameters; the dense layer sees $4 \times 4 \times 16 = 256$ inputs.

byKey.no-bias: Each filter and each class has a bias.
byKey.no-pool-shrink: You fed the dense layer the 1,024 values before pooling. Pooling leaves 256.

explain.text: Pooling learns nothing. The dense layer has $256 \times 10 + 10 = 2{,}570$, so the net has 2,730 parameters: 94% of them in the last layer.

screens.title: How far a layer sees
screens.prose: The **receptive field** of an output is the patch of input it depends on. One 3 by 3 layer sees 3 by 3. A second 3 by 3 layer on top sees 3 by 3 of the first layer’s outputs, which together cover 5 by 5 pixels.
screens.question: Three 3 by 3 layers at stride 1: what is the side of the receptive field?

byKey.nine: You multiplied 3 by 3. Each layer widens the view by 2, not by a factor.

explain.text: Each 3 by 3 layer at stride 1 adds 2 to the side: 3, 5, 7. Three small layers see as far as one 7 by 7 layer with $3 \times 9 = 27$ weights per channel pair instead of 49.

screens.title: Biases and channels
screens.prose: A 5 by 5 convolution from 3 channels to 8 filters, with padding 2, runs on a 32 by 32 image. One colleague counts 208 parameters; another counts 8,792, with a bias for every output position.
screens.question: How many parameters does the layer really have?

hints.text: How many weights in one filter?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each filter has a 5 by 5 kernel per input channel and one bias.

byKey.no-cin: You gave each filter one 5 by 5 kernel. It needs one per input channel: $3 \times 25 = 75$ weights.
byKey.bias-per-position: You gave each of the $32 \times 32$ positions its own bias. A filter shares one bias across positions, as it shares its weights.

explain.text: Each filter: $3 \times 25 = 75$ weights and 1 bias. Eight filters: 608. The image size enters only the multiply-adds, never the parameters.

screens.title: Two counts per layer
screens.prose: $$\text{params} = c_{\text{out}}(c_{\text{in}}k^2 + 1), \qquad \text{multiply-adds} = (\text{positions}) \times k^2 c_{\text{in}} \times c_{\text{out}}.$$ Stacked layers widen the view: at stride 1 the receptive field is $1 + \sum (k_i - 1)$.
screens.question: Doubling the image side from 8 to 16 (padding kept "same") does what to a conv layer?

options.text: Parameters stay; multiply-adds go up 4 times

options.why: The kernels do not depend on the image size; only the number of positions does.
There are 4 times as many positions, each a full dot product.
Parameters never see the image size.

feedback.correct: Same weights, four times the positions.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which count has the image size in it?

explain.text: The positions go from 64 to 256, so the multiply-adds go from 9,216 to 36,864; the 160 parameters do not move.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Each filter has a $k \times k$ kernel for every input channel.

explain.text: `c_out * (c_in * k * k + 1)` and `n_in * n_out + n_out`. The 2-2-1 net gives $6 + 3 = 9$, as `stat-learning` counted.

screens.title: The receptive field in code
screens.prose: Write `receptive_field(layers)` for a list of `(k, s)` pairs. Each layer adds $(k - 1)$ times the product of the strides before it: a step of one output there is that many pixels of input.
screens.question: Write `receptive_field`.

widget.how: Submit runs 6 hidden tests. They use two and three 3 by 3 layers, and conv, pool, conv as in level 3. Then two strided layers, no layers, and one 5 by 5 layer.

mutants.symptom: Multiplies kernel sizes: two 3 by 3 layers would see 9 by 9.
Ignores the stride, so a layer after pooling seems to see too little.
Adds the kernel sizes, counting the shared centre pixel twice.

feedback.correct: Track the jump between neighbouring outputs, and add $(k - 1)$ jumps per layer.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Two 3 by 3 layers see 5 by 5: each adds 2.
byKey.test-3: After a 2 by 2 pool at stride 2, one step on the next layer is 2 pixels, so its 3 by 3 kernel adds $2 \times 2 = 4$.

explain.text: With strides, neighbouring outputs of deeper layers sit `jump` pixels apart, so a kernel of $k$ adds $(k - 1) \times$ `jump`. Conv, pool, conv: $1 + 2 + 1 + 2 \times 2 = 8$.

screens.title: A model on every stock every minute
screens.prose: A desk runs the 1-to-16 convolution on an 8 by 8 grid of features for each of 500 stocks, every minute. Counts of this kind are the first estimate of what a model costs to run, and of how much data it needs to fit.
screens.question: How many multiply-adds does that layer cost per minute?

feedback.generic: Not quite. One layer costs 9,216 per stock.

byKey.one-stock: That is one stock. The desk runs all 500.
byKey.params: That multiplies the whole net’s parameters by 500. Running costs are multiply-adds.

explain.text: $500 \times 9{,}216 = 4{,}608{,}000$ a minute, trivial for one layer. The 160 parameters say how much the layer must learn; the count of positions says what it costs every minute.

ideas: A conv layer has $c_{\text{out}}(c_{\text{in}}k^2 + 1)$ parameters whatever the image size; a dense layer $n_{\text{in}}n_{\text{out}} + n_{\text{out}}$. For the same shapes: 160 against 66,560.
Multiply-adds are positions times $k^2 c_{\text{in}}$ times $c_{\text{out}}$: 9,216 for the 1-to-16 layer on 8 by 8. Parameters say what a layer learns, multiply-adds what it costs.
The level 3 net has $160 + 0 + 2{,}570 = 2{,}730$ parameters; a 64-40-10 MLP has 3,010. At stride 1 each $k \times k$ layer adds $k - 1$ to the receptive field: 5, then 7.

formula.name: Parameters of a conv layer
formula.note: One bias per filter; no image size.

summary.trap: A bias per position, or a kernel without its input channels, gives the wrong count.

quiz.question: A 1 by 1 convolution from 64 channels to 32. How many parameters?

byKey.no-bias: Each of the 32 filters has a bias.
byKey.k-not-one: That is a 3 by 3 kernel. Here $k^2 = 1$.

explain.text: $k^2 = 1$, so each filter has 64 weights and a bias: 2,080.

quiz.question: Four 3 by 3 layers at stride 1. What is the side of the receptive field?

byKey.product: You multiplied the kernel sides. Each layer adds $k - 1$.

quiz.question: A 3 by 3 convolution from 8 to 8 channels on a 16 by 16 map with padding 1. How many multiply-adds?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Positions times $k^2 c_{\text{in}}$ times $c_{\text{out}}$.

byKey.one-channel: Each dot product runs over all 8 input channels.

explain.text: 256 positions, each a dot product of $9 \times 8 = 72$ terms, for 8 filters: 147,456.
